The Pope and the Path Forward

Share
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 4:34
Instaread

At CatholicVote, we intend to lean even further into the Catholic dimension of our mission as we establish new coalitions that can help us build a more just society. The Church herself offers a vision of the future for our nation: a call to higher truths and the common good.

Providentially, that vision is being charted right now by Pope Leo XIV. In the Canary Islands he mentioned the “right of migrants to remain,” challenging the view that a new place is the only or best option. In Spain, he fearlessly called out the duty of the state to protect the unborn. In Uruguay, he insisted that protecting the unborn children and supporting the parents who welcome them are inseparable responsibilities.

In Argentina, he reminded leaders that prosperity means little if families cannot provide for their households or if young people must leave their homeland for opportunity. In Peru, he reaffirmed that the family is the first natural society—existing before the state, with its own rights. He has made the Catholic case for policies that nurture the family, the basic building block of society.

Life is more complicated than politics

In the U.S. we have become accustomed to treating the most important questions facing our country as separate political debates.

Abortion is one issue. The economy is another. Parental rights, education, housing affordability, and religious freedom are placed in different categories, fought over by different coalitions, and too often reduced to competing partisan priorities.

But most families do not experience life that way.

A young couple deciding whether to have their first child does not necessarily separate the price of housing from the value of parenthood. Parents struggling to make ends meet do not separate their children’s education from the freedom to raise them according to their convictions.

A mother facing an unexpected pregnancy needs more than the assurance that her unborn child has a right to life. She also needs a community to stand beside her and a society in which welcoming that child does not mean surrendering hope for her own future.

A young person needs more than a career path: he needs confidence in the future, the ability to find honor in his work, and to answer the question of what affordability is intended to provide.

We need more than a GDP that serves the S&P 500. We need a vision of what human flourishing is and that vision is tied together by the pursuit of the greatest good, God, and one of the most amazing ways His love is revealed—the family.

Rebuilding a new coalition by focusing on innate aspirations

The desire to love and be loved, to build a home, to welcome children, to protect the vulnerable, and to leave something good to the next generation is written into the human heart. These aspirations belong to every American, regardless of religion, background, or political allegiance.

And that is why I believe there is such an enormous reason for hope.

Our recent elections delivered painful disappointments. But electoral defeats do not invalidate moral truths. And political coalitions, unlike those truths, can and must be rebuilt. But they must be rebuilt around a more coherent vision of the future, which passes through the family.

The lesson is not that we should abandon our convictions. It is that we must do a better job of showing our fellow Americans how those convictions speak to their deepest hopes and most urgent concerns.

There is hope for the future

Young Americans are rediscovering the Christian faith and searching for a more enduring foundation for their lives.

Hispanic families are looking for leaders who understand both their economic struggles, their commitment to their children, and the longing for a better future that deeply incorporate their family values.

And growing numbers of parents, including many who do not identify with traditional political movements, are questioning a culture of consumerism, dependency, and relentless technological distraction that too often undermines family life.

These Americans are searching for a political home. And many share a fundamental intuition: something precious about our humanity is being lost, and it is worth recovering.

The crowds that welcomed Pope Leo in South America remind us of something our increasingly cynical political culture tends to forget: the human heart still responds to truth, to goodness, and to the promise of hope.

That is what we must offer. Hope for families.

Our children must never inherit a country that has lost the courage to welcome its own future. Together, we can build something better.
